events.title: COP31 climate conference ends without fossil fuel consensus for first time since 2009
events.one_liner: COP31, held in Antalya, Turkey in November 2026, concluded without a consensus cover decision for the first time since 2009. The conference, which ran two days beyond its scheduled end date, failed to reach agreement on an overarching statement due to deep divisions over whether fossil fuels and carbon capture should be mentioned, and disagreements on climate financing levels from developed to developing nations. Countries did adopt several decisions including a program to help workers and communities transition away from fossil fuels and a plan to assess climate adaptation progress. The European Union, several Latin American countries, and Pacific Island states rejected the proposed text. A central aim was to set voluntary global goals for economic electrification and increase funding for developing countries to adapt to climate impacts. This outcome follows the 2023 Dubai agreement where delegates first agreed that a "just and orderly" transition away from fossil fuels is needed to slow global warming. The Marshall Islands climate envoy stated the country would not accept "false solutions" to compromise on the agreement.

events.title: President of the United States endorses Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia leadership

The president emphasized that Nvidia's reinstatement of Huang was necessary for the company's success and the American economy. events.title: FBI and USDA databases hit by separate cyber intrusions
events.one_liner: On November 23, 2026, separate cyber intrusions compromised core databases at both the FBI and the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The FBI is investigating an intrusion into the National Crime Information Center (NCIC), a database used by local, state, and federal law enforcement to share records on fugitives, warrants, missing persons, stolen property, and criminal background checks. The scope and identity of attackers remain unknown. This marks the bureau's third security probe in 2026, following an investigation into suspicious activity on an internal surveillance and investigative records system in March and a September breach by cybercrime group ShinyHunters that compromised an FBI jobs portal and exposed personal data of approximately 38,000 staff members and applicants. In a separate incident, hackers penetrated a USDA database used to send financial payments to farmers. The USDA notified employees of the breach on Thursday. Two former USDA officials warned that while the breach appeared contained to the payment system, the compromised network could serve as a backdoor into food safety records and animal-borne disease research. Neither agency nor the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency responded to comment requests. Attackers remain unidentified. The breaches followed a week of technical outages across banking and air traffic control, though federal officials attributed those disruptions to routine system upgrades and vulnerability patching rather than cyberattacks, with no immediate indication the outages are linked to the FBI or USDA intrusions. The incidents coincided with the departure of White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross.

events.title: Anthropic researcher announces AI-assisted proof of Riemann hypothesis
events.one_liner: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, announced on November 20, 2026, that he has discovered a proof of the Riemann hypothesis using Anthropic's Claude AI. The Riemann hypothesis, first proposed in 1859 by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann, is one of mathematics' most famous unsolved problems and is worth a $1 million Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize. The hypothesis proposes that prime numbers follow a specific pattern along the number line. Alpöge's Claude-assisted proof runs to more than 250,000 pages and has been formalized in Lean, a computer programming language used to mechanically verify proofs. The Lean code verification is over 17 million lines long. The proof was subsequently verified by independent researchers. Alpöge stated he also believes the proof confirms the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, a broader expansion of Riemann's conjecture. The announcement caps a year during which AI systems from OpenAI and Anthropic made breakthroughs on numerous open mathematical problems, including OpenAI's solutions to the Navier-Stokes problem and over 700 papers claiming solutions to 372 open problems. This announcement came one day after Anthropic's stock market debut.

events.title: Ransomware attacks surge 38% in Q3 2026 as exploit techniques escalate
events.one_liner: Ransomware incidents increased 38% quarter-over-quarter in Q3 2026, according to Beazley Security's Threat Report. Vulnerability exploitation doubled to account for 28% of initial access in ransomware cases, compared to 14% in Q2 2026. Malware accounted for 19% of initial access incidents in Q3, up from 14% in Q2. Nearly 37,000 Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) were published during Q3 2026, an increase of almost 80% from the prior quarter. Attackers increasingly targeted internet-facing applications, cloud credentials, and overlooked systems. AI agents conducted largely automated intrusions involving vulnerability exploitation, lateral movement, and data theft. Attackers bypassed multi-factor authentication (MFA) through stolen sessions and device-code phishing. Beazley Security recommended prioritizing known exploited vulnerabilities, internet-facing applications, and systems providing access to credentials, cloud infrastructure, or critical business operations.

events.title: Pegasus lunar terrain vehicle passes NASA PDR, scheduled for 2028 moon launch
events.one_liner: Lunar Outpost's Pegasus Lunar Terrain Vehicle passed NASA's Preliminary Design Review (PDR) on November 23, 2026, becoming the first LTV to clear this milestone. The vehicle, derived from an earlier design called Eagle, is scheduled to launch to the Moon in 2028. Pegasus underwent human-in-the-loop testing with suited astronauts from Johnson Space Center, evaluating design, usability, comfort, soil mechanics, traction, and mobility with spring mesh tires. The company built three prototypes for these tests. Following PDR approval, Lunar Outpost plans to test a drivable version in simulated lunar environments, with and without NASA astronauts. Flight-ready delivery to NASA is planned for late 2027. The rover is expected to map lunar surface terrain at approximately 3.7 miles (6 km) per day and will be remotely operated initially before human missions. It will support up to three moonwalks per Artemis mission. NASA's LTV requirements include carrying up to 176 pounds (80 kg) of lunar material and tools and traveling up to six miles (10 km) on a single charge. The Pegasus is backed by $220 million in NASA funding and built on lessons from the Mobile Autonomous Prospecting Platform (MAPP) rover sent to the Moon in 2025. Astrolab's competing design, the Crewed Lunar Vehicle 1 (CLV-1), delivered a mockup to Axiom Space for evaluation by Artemis astronauts.

events.title: Critical binary-parser vulnerability enables JavaScript code injection
events.one_liner: A critical code injection vulnerability has been disclosed in the binary-parser library, tracked as CVE-2026-134814 with a CVSS score of 9.2 (also referenced as 8.1). The flaw affects binary-parser versions prior to 2.3.1 and allows attackers who control parser definitions to execute arbitrary JavaScript code in the Node.js process. The vulnerability stems from insufficient validation of user-controlled string options (length, lengthInBytes, key, tag, offset, and values passed to namely()) that are inserted directly into generated JavaScript code without proper sanitization. According to maintainer Keichi Takahashi, the affected options are now validated as identifier paths (e.g., foo, $parent.len), with expressions like 'len - 1' rejected in favor of functions. This is an incomplete fix for the earlier CVE-2026-1245 (CVSS 6.5), a similar code injection vulnerability disclosed in January 2026. Parsing untrusted binary data with a trusted parser definition is not affected. An advisory was released by the project maintainer on November 11, 2026. Users are advised to update to version 2.3.1 or later.

events.title: UN climate talks collapse for first time in 17 years over fossil fuel language
events.one_liner: The UN climate conference ended without an agreement for the first time in 17 years on November 23, 2026. Negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed over language on fossil fuels. The European Union, Latin America, and Pacific island nations objected to a proposal by petrostates—led by Saudi Arabia and Russia—to omit mention of fossil fuels from the final agreement. Irish environment minister Darragh O'Brien said it was "unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no reference to fossil fuels." The rejected draft also included no firm commitments from wealthy countries to fund a climate reparations fund for poorer nations established in 2022. The United States did not send an official delegation to the conference; since the president of the United States returned to office, the U.S. has moved to pull out of the UN climate treaty. Under UN climate process rules, any agreement requires consensus approval, giving every country—including major fossil fuel producers—effective veto power. Former vice president Al Gore called for reforming the process "to stop polluters from blocking progress." Climate Analytics head Bill Hare noted that countries refusing to accept the document "drew a line in the sand" by rejecting a pact with no reference to phasing out fossil fuels.

events.title: Critical ScreenConnect Flaw Exploited to Hijack MSP Technician Systems
events.one_liner: Threat actors are exploiting CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS 9.9), a critical vulnerability in ConnectWise ScreenConnect, to compromise managed service provider (MSP) technician workstations. The flaw allows a guest to transfer and execute malicious payloads on a connecting technician's host. Between October 20 and November 16, 2026, Huntress researchers observed at least 688,000 guest "run file" requests targeting 42 ScreenConnect servers from 29 IP addresses, with attackers spraying servers blindly using filenames like update.bat or update_<8 hex>.bat. In one documented case on November 12, 2026, a technician's workstation was exploited to run a guest-pushed batch file (update_224ac089.bat) that decoded a Telegram bot token, downloaded a malicious MSI installer masquerading as "WindowsUpdate.msi" from masterdarky[.]com, and launched a rogue ScreenConnect client pointing to an attacker relay—all within approximately 9 seconds. The batch script registered the infection with a Telegram bot. Attackers also used canary files (marker.txt) to test payload delivery and targeted attacks where batch scripts were dropped into the Windows Startup folder. The attackers obtained publicly downloadable ScreenConnect Access installers to extract relay addresses, registered unauthorized guest clients with victim servers, and created fake sessions with cryptocurrency exchange-themed names (BITMEX-BOT, KUCOIN-SRV, LAPTOP-BINANCE) to trick technicians into connecting. This activity is distinct from a separate attack wave involving SCKit malware deployment through authentication flaws in third-party ScreenConnect extensions.

events.title: GPT-6.2 Astra Solves Previously Unsolved Math Theorem and Invents Novel Proof Strategy
events.one_liner: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra solved Smoktunowicz's gap theorem (a 2006 mathematical theorem), producing the first known formalized, machine-verifiable proof written in Lean programming language without human assistance. The theorem states that when a mathematical system multiplies its basic building blocks, growth is either quite slow or very fast with no middle ground. Because key foundations from the original proof were missing from the Mathlib math library, Astra independently developed a novel proof strategy using "capacity," a metric from existing research that measures the minimum number of elements added per computation step, rather than following the published mathematical proofs. The proof was 1,800 lines long. Astra completed this task on Autoform-Hard, a subset of Meta FAIR's AutoformBench containing 56 tasks that ten models in Meta's study failed to solve within budget. After initially attempting to quit at 47 minutes and eight dollars, the system rejected the attempt since unsolved submissions require at least $20 spent. After nine minutes of searching for a new strategy with no code input, Astra delivered the proof at the 94-minute mark, costing $21.58 total. Astra now leads the Autoform-Hard leaderboard with 49 solved tasks, ahead of GPT-6.2 Sol and Claude Fable 5.2, which each solved 48 tasks.

events.title: OpenAI publishes AI progress chart and proposes shared safety limits across labs
events.one_liner: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published a post on November 22, 2026, titled 'Perplexity and Intelligence' proposing that AI laboratories adopt a voluntary shared safety limit based on perplexity (a metric measuring how well a model predicts the next word). The proposal includes a progress chart tracking OpenAI's models: GPT-4 scored roughly 0.91 perplexity; Pachocki notes that once losses fell below 0.8, transformative capabilities emerged in cybersecurity and mathematics; he expects further capability jumps in a 0.68 to 0.7 window. The proposal asks labs to pledge not to exceed a set perplexity threshold until safety monitoring and AI behavior understanding reach concrete milestones. No lab has formally agreed, and no binding cap exists. Pachocki frames transparency about OpenAI's position as justified by the urgency of establishing shared industry safety measures, though he acknowledges limitations: different labs use different datasets, perplexity does not map neatly to tasks people care about, and chain-of-thought reasoning can increase capability without changing the perplexity score.

events.title: Ancient quasar pair from cosmic dawn defies galaxy formation models
events.one_liner: Astronomers discovered Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua (officially J1602+4228AB), the oldest known compact pair of quasars, existing 900 million years after the Big Bang. The two black holes powering the quasars have masses of 1.5 billion and 400 million solar masses respectively. The pair holds the record for the closest separation between two known quasars from cosmic dawn. Their rapid growth to such massive sizes in the early universe contradicts current galaxy formation models, which cannot explain how black holes became so large so quickly. The discovery combined observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea, Hawaii. Research was led by Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab, and published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters. Paired quasars are theoretically expected to be relatively common due to frequent galaxy encounters and mergers, but finding and studying them is exceptionally difficult, making this close pair from such an early cosmic epoch particularly remarkable.

events.title: Acute myeloid leukemia originates 50+ years before diagnosis, study reveals
events.one_liner: Researchers at the University of Cambridge and University College London discovered that acute myeloid leukemia (AML) can begin developing over 50 years before diagnosis. The study, published in Nature, analyzed blood samples from women in the UK Collaborative Trial of Ovarian Cancer Screening (UKCTOCS), examining 47 women who developed AML (average diagnosis age 72) and 46 women who remained cancer-free. In two-thirds of cases, the first cancer-driving genetic mutation appeared before age 20 and remained largely unnoticed for decades. The research used DNA sequencing and mathematical modeling to work backward and determine when mutations first emerged, how quickly affected cells multiplied, and how they competed with other blood cells as disease approached. Mutated cells grew in predictable patterns that accelerated as additional mutations accumulated. The findings suggest doctors may eventually identify people at risk years or decades before symptoms appear, potentially enabling prevention by slowing abnormal blood cell growth. AML is an aggressive blood cancer affecting approximately 2,700 people annually in the UK, with only about one in six patients surviving at least five years after diagnosis.

events.title: Investigation: Russians with Criminal Records Obtained Romanian Passports by Posing as Ukrainians
events.one_liner: An investigation by the Kyiv Independent and partner newsrooms (Public Record Romania, Cu Sens Moldova, Follow the Money Netherlands, Le Monde France, and the Investigative Center of Ján Kuciak Slovakia) published November 23, 2026, found that Russian nationals with criminal records obtained EU passports by fraudulently posing as Ukrainians and exploiting Romania's citizenship laws. Researchers reviewed court files from 55 civil cases involving disputed Romanian identity documents; more than 30 beneficiaries were Russian citizens, including individuals sanctioned by Ukraine for ties to Russia's war machine or organized crime. At least eight Russian citizens posed as Ukrainians to obtain Romanian documents during Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine, all receiving assistance from the same notary in Moldova. Romanian authorities charged at least 16 Russian citizens with using forged documents to obtain Romanian passports. A Romanian court is hearing over 800 civil cases to annul identity documents obtained with forged papers. These fraudulent schemes exploited Romania's repatriation process, allowing beneficiaries to obtain authentic Romanian birth certificates using forged citizenship certificates, which then enabled acquisition of genuine Romanian passports conferring EU citizenship and visa-free travel across Europe. Among identified Russian beneficiaries: a member of a powerful Chechen clan, the then-head of a Russian state-owned explosives manufacturer, and an individual linked to organized crime reports.

events.title: Archaeologists reveal Iron Age British ruler Verica may have been a woman
events.one_liner: Archaeologists from Bournemouth University have presented evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile around AD 40 triggered Rome's invasion of Britain in AD 43, was female rather than male as traditionally assumed. Verica ruled the Atrebates tribe across Hampshire and West Sussex. After being forced from power, Verica fled to Rome and appealed to Emperor Claudius for assistance; Roman historian Cassius Dio recorded that this appeal motivated Claudius to invade Britain. Dr. Miles Russell, Director of Archaeological Fieldwork at Bournemouth University, identifies three lines of evidence for Verica's female identity: the name Verica ends in "a," consistent with female names of the era (similar to Cartimandua and Boudica); coins issued under Verica's rule bear the Latin title "rex," which Russell argues is gender-neutral and was used by both male and female rulers recognized by Rome, including Cleopatra of Egypt; and artistic impressions depict Verica in Iron Age dress with Roman-style accessories including gold jewelry and a Julio-Claudian hairstyle. Russell attributes the historical misidentification to the patriarchal bias of 19th-century classical historians.

events.title: Self-modifying AI models can edit their own weights
events.one_liner: Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign report that a 27B parameter open language model can rewrite its own weights without gradients or fresh training runs, with edits that persist in the checkpoint. The model performs a concrete loop: reads failures, proposes a weight edit, tests it, and retains only edits that pass. On held-out math problems, the model achieved +6.6 accuracy points on 490 pre-registered tasks across eight sequential self-edit sessions. On image benchmarks, the model repaired performance from 7% to ~70% after matrix noise corruption. The 27B scale was necessary—smaller models at 2B, 4B, and 9B failed or self-broke during the process. The work required only one GPU and hours of compute rather than a full training cluster. The research is documented in arXiv:2611.21885 and titled "Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights."

events.title: OpenAI chief scientist proposes perplexity-based 'red line' for AI development
events.one_liner: OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki published an essay on November 22, 2026, proposing perplexity—a metric measuring how accurately a model predicts the next token—as a unified, cross-company standard for measuring AI model capability. On this basis, he proposed setting an industry-wide "red line" or development ceiling that would prevent developers from crossing an agreed capability threshold until monitoring and understanding capabilities reach clear milestones. Pachocki did not specify what value the first red line should be set at or when it would take effect. He disclosed internal OpenAI data showing GPT-3.5 at log-perplexity of approximately 0.99 and GPT-4 at approximately 0.91. He indicated that transformative capabilities in cybersecurity and mathematics emerge below 0.8 log-perplexity, with breakthroughs on open math problems occurring at around 0.76. Pachocki warned that AI could drive rapid pre-training progress as early as 2027, while alignment and monitoring progress is unlikely to keep pace. CEO Sam Altman publicly endorsed the proposal, calling it "one of the most important things OpenAI has published in some time." The proposal comes as Democrats, following U.S. midterm elections, prepare to strengthen AI regulation, while the president of the United States opposes broad restrictions.

Investigations at Nowy Lipowiec and Rudnik were completed; the Mołodycz investigation was scheduled to finish on November 23. During the incursion, a Swedish Air Force pilot flying a JAS 39 Gripen fighter jet under NATO command was authorized to shoot down a suspected Russian cruise missile over Poland but did not fire due to severe weather preventing target identification. The incident coincided with military exercises in Poland involving British and French troops from the so-called Coalition of the Willing. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned Russia's attacks and stressed the alliance would continue supporting Ukraine. Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz described it as one of the largest attacks since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. Moldova and Finland also reported separate airspace violations by Russia on November 21.

events.title: Claude AI helps resolve famous Riemann problem
events.one_liner: Two independent groups verified an Anthropic mathematician's Claude-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as of November 22, 2026. The Riemann Hypothesis, nearly 170 years old, concerns how evenly prime numbers appear en route to infinity. A Fields Medal winner told Nature that if the proof fully checks out, "it is clearly a historic milestone in mathematics" and expressed belief it is "likely to be correct." The development follows OpenAI's release of more than 300 mathematical proofs developed with human oversight. A mathematics professor characterized the achievement as an example of "a very skillful jockey riding a really fast horse," suggesting AI-assisted mathematical proof-finding may become more common.

The research estimated that approximately 4.7 per 1,000 people with type 2 diabetes develop Alzheimer's disease annually. The study, titled "Incidence and risk of Alzheimer's disease in individuals with type 2 diabetes: a systematic review and meta-analysis," was published in Alzheimer's Research & Therapy in 2026. Lead researcher Dr. Emmanuel Adewuyi from Curtin School of Population Health noted that this review differed from previous analyses by focusing specifically on type 2 diabetes and Alzheimer's disease (rather than combining multiple diabetes types or dementia forms) and by measuring both relative risk and incidence of new cases to provide a clearer picture of Alzheimer's burden in the type 2 diabetes population.

events.title: NASA's Voyager 1 Reaches Historic Milestone One Light-Day from Earth
events.one_liner: NASA's Voyager 1 reached a historic milestone on November 18, 2026, at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST), becoming the first spacecraft to travel one light-day from Earth. A light-day is the distance light travels in one day, approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). After 49 years in space, Voyager 1 is now so distant that radio signals from Earth take a full 24 hours to reach it. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory received a radio signal from Voyager 1 on Thursday, exactly 24 hours after the spacecraft reached the milestone, confirming the achievement. Despite the milestone, Voyager 1 has experienced a technical problem; NASA engineers have not received science or engineering data from the spacecraft since November 14, though it continues to transmit a carrier signal. The probe was launched by NASA in 1977 as part of the Voyager mission, which explored the outer planets during a rare planetary alignment.
